title: Product Names Containing A Digit
description:
Report the `name` of every product whose name contains at least one digit, using `GLOB` (not `LIKE`).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql: SELECT name FROM products WHERE name GLOB '*[0-9]*';
outputExplanation: None of the product names (Keyboard, Mouse, Desk, Lamp) contain a digit, so the result is empty. A hidden test with products named P1 and P2 demonstrates this query working.
hint: SQLite's LIKE has no character-class syntax, but GLOB does — `[0-9]` inside a GLOB pattern matches any single digit, same idea as a tiny regex.

title: Employee Names Containing The Letter A
description:
Report the `name` of every employee whose name contains the letter `a` **anywhere**, case-insensitively (not just at the start).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE LOWER(name) LIKE '%a%';
outputExplanation: Ava, Cara, Dan, Gia and Hal all contain the letter 'a' in their names. Ben, Eve and Finn do not and are excluded.
hint: A leading and trailing `%` means "anywhere in the string" — anchoring only the start (`'a%'`) or only the end (`'%a'`) would answer a different question.

title: Hires Per Calendar Quarter
description:
Report how many employees were hired in each calendar quarter (`Q1` = Jan-Mar, `Q2` = Apr-Jun, `Q3` = Jul-Sep, `Q4` = Oct-Dec), across all years combined.

Name the columns `quarter` and `hires`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 1 AND 3 THEN 'Q1'
    WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 4 AND 6 THEN 'Q2'
    WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 7 AND 9 THEN 'Q3'
    ELSE 'Q4'
  END AS quarter,
  COUNT(*) AS hires
FROM employees
GROUP BY quarter;
outputExplanation: Four employees were hired in Q1 (January-March), one in Q2, two in Q3 and one in Q4.
hint: strftime('%m', ...) returns the month as zero-padded text ('04') — CAST it to INTEGER before comparing with BETWEEN, or the comparison happens on the wrong type.

title: Fiscal Year Labels (Year Starts In April)
description:
This company's fiscal year runs from **April 1st to March 31st** — so a hire on 2022-01-15 belongs to fiscal year `FY2021`, not `FY2022`. Report every employee's `name` and their fiscal year label.

Name the columns `name` and `fiscal_year`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name,
  'FY' || (CASE
    WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) >= 4 THEN CAST(strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS INTEGER)
    ELSE CAST(strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS INTEGER) - 1
  END) AS fiscal_year
FROM employees;
outputExplanation: Ava (Jan 2018) gets FY2017, Ben and Cara (Mar 2019) get FY2018, Gia (Feb 2022) gets FY2021 — all hired before April roll back one fiscal year. Dan (Jul 2021) and Eve (Nov 2017) stay in their calendar year's FY.
hint: January through March belong to the *previous* calendar year's fiscal year — the classic off-by-one this kind of bucketing trips people up on.

title: Short Product Codes Or Missing Category
description:
Report the `name` of every product whose name looks like a short product code — exactly two letters followed by one digit, like `P1` or `B2` — **or** whose `category` is currently unknown (`NULL`).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: No product has a two-letter-one-digit code name or a NULL category in this dataset, so the result is empty. A hidden test demonstrates the NULL category case.
hint: GLOB has no length-anchoring shortcut like LIKE's underscore count implies here by construction — three single-character classes back to back means "exactly three characters, this shape", nothing shorter or longer will match.

title: Clean Up Messy Customer Names
description:
`source_orders.customer_name` has inconsistent formatting — extra whitespace, inconsistent casing. Report the distinct set of customer names after trimming leading/trailing whitespace and lowercasing.

Name the column `customer`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql: SELECT DISTINCT LOWER(TRIM(customer_name)) AS customer FROM source_orders;
outputExplanation: After trimming and lowercasing, the four distinct names are 'ann lee', 'ben kim', 'cy ortiz' and 'dee fox'. A hidden test shows that TRIM removes leading/trailing spaces from names like '  ben kim '.
hint: TRIM only removes leading/trailing whitespace, not whitespace in the middle — that's enough here since the mess in this dataset is only at the edges and in casing.

title: Hired On The Last Day Of The Month
description:
Report the `name` of every employee hired on the last calendar day of their hire month (the 28th, 29th, 30th or 31st, whichever is correct for that specific month).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE hire_date = date(hire_date, 'start of month', '+1 month', '-1 day');
outputExplanation: None of the 8 hire dates fall on the last day of their month, so the result is empty. Hidden tests demonstrate June 30 and February 29 (leap year) as qualifying last-day hires.
hint: Don't hardcode `'-31'` or check against a fixed day number — months have different lengths (and February has 28 or 29). Compute "the day before the start of next month" instead, and SQLite's date() modifiers handle the varying month lengths for you.

title: Calendar Days With Zero Orders
description:
Considering the full range from the earliest to the latest `order_date` in `orders`, report every calendar date **in that range** on which no order was placed at all.

Name the column `missing_date`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE spine(d) AS (
  SELECT MIN(order_date) FROM orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(d, '+1 day') FROM spine WHERE d < (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders)
)
SELECT d AS missing_date
FROM spine
WHERE d IS NOT NULL
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.order_date = d);
outputExplanation: Only 6 dates between January 10, 2022 and January 2, 2023 have orders. Every other calendar day in that range — over 300 dates — had no orders and is reported.
hint: There's no table of "all possible dates" to join against, so build one: a recursive CTE that starts at the earliest date and adds one day at a time up to the latest. Guard against an empty orders table, where MIN/MAX are both NULL.

title: Fiscal Quarter Labels Across The Year Boundary
description:
Same fiscal year as before (starts April 1st), but now report each employee's full fiscal quarter label, e.g. `FY2021-Q4` for a hire in January 2022 (fiscal Q4 of FY2021, since FY2021 runs April 2021 through March 2022).

Name the columns `name` and `fiscal_quarter`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name,
  'FY' || (CASE WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) >= 4
           THEN CAST(strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS INTEGER)
           ELSE CAST(strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS INTEGER) - 1 END)
  || '-Q' ||
  (CASE
     WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 4 AND 6 THEN 1
     WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 7 AND 9 THEN 2
     WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', hire_date) AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 10 AND 12 THEN 3
     ELSE 4
   END) AS fiscal_quarter
FROM employees;
outputExplanation: Ava (Jan 2018) gets FY2017-Q4, Eve (Nov 2017) gets FY2017-Q3, and Dan (Jul 2021) gets FY2021-Q2. Each employee's label reflects the fiscal year rules and which quarter their hire month falls in.
hint: The fiscal year part uses the same Jan-Mar-rolls-back-a-year logic as before. The quarter number is independent of that: Apr-Jun is always fiscal Q1, regardless of which calendar year it happened to fall in.

title: Names With The Letter A At Least Twice
description:
SQLite has no regular-expression function built in. Report the `name` of every employee whose name contains the letter `a` (case-insensitive) **at least twice**.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE LENGTH(LOWER(name)) - LENGTH(REPLACE(LOWER(name), 'a', '')) >= 2;
outputExplanation: Ava and Cara each contain the letter 'a' twice. Dan, Gia and Hal contain it only once, and Ben, Eve and Finn have none.
hint: A classic no-regex trick: REPLACE every 'a' with nothing, then the drop in LENGTH tells you exactly how many 'a's were removed — no counting loop needed.
